name: Anton Valukas

summary.text: Anton R. Valukas, then chairman of the Chicago law firm Jenner & Block and a former U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, was appointed in January 2009 by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York as examiner in the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy. His report, dated March 11, 2010 and running more than 2,200 pages, found that Lehman used 'Repo 105' transactions to remove about $50 billion of assets from its balance sheet at the end of the first and second quarters of 2008 without disclosure, that colorable claims existed against auditor Ernst & Young, and that former CEO Richard Fuld was at least grossly negligent in causing Lehman to file misleading periodic reports.

facts.claim: In January 2009 Valukas, chairman of Jenner & Block and a former U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois in the late 1980s, was named court-appointed examiner in the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy, subject to approval by the bankruptcy court.
facts.quote: a former federal prosecutor known for his aggressive stance on white-collar crime during a four-year stint as U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois in the late 1980s

Anton R. Valukas

facts.claim: Valukas was appointed by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York to examine the causes of Lehman's failure, with Jenner & Block as counsel to the examiner.
facts.quote: Counsel to the Examiner was Jenner & Block LLP.

sources.title: Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. Chapter 11 Proceedings Examiner's Report
Lehman executives cause of failure - examiner's report

facts.claim: The examiner's report found that Lehman used Repo 105 transactions, structured to be treated as sales under accounting rules, to remove about $50 billion of assets from its balance sheet at the end of the first and second quarters of 2008, and that the practice was not disclosed, even to Lehman's board.
facts.quote: Lehman used these transactions to remove about $50 billion of assets from its balance sheet at the end of the first and second quarters of 2008.

facts.claim: The report found enough evidence to support at least three colorable claims against Ernst & Young for not looking more closely into Lehman's accounting; it said Ernst & Young first learned of Repo 105 in 2001 and by 2007 was aware of $29 billion in Repo 105 transactions. Ernst & Young pointed to the report's conclusion that it made no finding that Lehman's assets or liabilities were improperly valued in its November 30, 2007 financial statements.
facts.quote: According to the report, Ernst first learned of Lehman's use of Repo 105 in 2001, shortly after it was designed. By 2007, Ernst was aware of $29 billion in Repo 105 transactions.

facts.claim: The report stated that former Lehman CEO Richard Fuld was 'at least grossly negligent' in causing Lehman to file misleading periodic reports, and described Lehman's conduct as ranging from serious but non-culpable errors of business judgment to actionable balance sheet manipulation.
facts.quote: the report said Richard Fuld was "at least grossly negligent" in causing Lehman to file misleading periodic reports

facts.claim: The New York Attorney General sued Ernst & Young in December 2010 under the Martin Act over Lehman's Repo 105 transactions, and in April 2015 announced a $10 million settlement; the office said Ernst & Young separately paid about $99 million to settle a private federal class action.
facts.quote: Ernst & Young paid some $99 million to settle a private federal class action that relied in part on facts uncovered by the Attorney General's investigation

openQuestions: Site claim that Valukas 'uncovered the Repo 105 accounting scheme' and that the examiner found colorable claims against Ernst & Young over non-disclosure of up to $50 billion in quarter-end Repo 105 usage: supported by the report and contemporaneous coverage.

Site claim that Ernst & Young paid $10 million to the New York Attorney General and $99 million to investors without admitting wrongdoing: the amounts are supported by the Attorney General's 2015 release; the 'without admitting wrongdoing' wording was not confirmed.

Site claims about the Linklaters English-law opinion and the use of Lehman Brothers International (Europe) for Repo 105 were not covered by the sources returned, though they are the subject of Volume 3 of the report.
A later bankruptcy disclosure statement gives the report's filing date as February 8, 2010 while the public release is dated March 11, 2010; the sealed filing and public unsealing dates may differ.
